posts.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: The 2024 U.S. midterm elections saw a surge of anti‑data‑center sentiment, with voters rejecting dozens of ballot measures that would have eased approvals for new facilities. The shift coincided with Democrats gaining control of key state legislatures, including Texas, where governor‑elect Gina Hinojosa pledged to curb data‑center expansion. Elon Musk’s $500 million donation to Republicans did not translate into favorable outcomes for his data‑center interests, as his companies now face a more hostile regulatory climate. In response, firms like OpenAI announced a “compute campus” policy that removes NDAs and rebrands data centers to address public concerns.
key_points: The midterms amplified grassroots opposition to data‑center construction, leading to widespread ballot measure defeats.
Elon Musk’s political donations failed to protect his data‑center interests amid a new Democratic‑led regulatory environment.
Tech companies are shifting strategies, with OpenAI rebranding data centers as compute campuses and increasing transparency to appease voters.
The election’s outcome signals a tougher future for hyperscalers, potentially affecting investment and expansion plans.

posts.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: A U.S. intelligence memo alleged that Alice Huang, a technology executive at Singapore‑based Megaspeed, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and that the two had a romantic relationship. The memo was first reported by the New York Times and later by the Financial Times, prompting Nvidia to deny that any classified information was shared and to describe the interactions as "not unusual." A separate New York Times investigation highlighted New Matrix, a Chinese firm authorized to buy Nvidia chips, whose office appeared to be a shell, raising concerns it could be a front for a blacklisted private‑equity firm. The story has intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s China ambitions and the CEO’s ties to alleged Chinese intelligence.
key_points: U.S. intelligence memo claims Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
The memo also alleges a romantic relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang
Nvidia denies sharing classified information and says the interactions were normal

posts.title: Sequoia shutting down its Scouts program marks the end of an era | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anna Heim
posts.summary: Sequoia announced a broad overhaul that includes closing its London office and shutting down its long‑running scout program, a move that signals a shift in how VCs source deals. The scout model, pioneered by Sequoia 17 years ago, has been adopted by many firms but is now seen as reaching its limits amid increased competition for deal flow. While Sequoia framed the decision as a need for greater focus rather than a critique of scouts, other firms like a16z are already revamping their own networks to concentrate on a smaller, more active group of scouts. The closure may prompt other funds to rethink or restructure their scouting initiatives, though the broader ecosystem benefits from the experience and network building that scouts have historically provided.
key_points: Sequoia is ending its scout program as part of a broader focus shift.
The scout model, once a pioneer, is now considered to have reached its limits amid deal‑flow competition.
Other VC firms, such as a16z, are already tightening their scout networks, suggesting a trend toward more selective scouting.

posts.title: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Amazon has launched a new text‑based interface that lets U.S. customers chat with its Alexa AI agent to shop on Amazon, a move that follows the company’s earlier decision to block Meta’s Muse from accessing its site.  The feature, rolled out just before the holiday shopping season, allows users to search for items, add them to a cart, place orders, manage lists, compare products, and even upload pictures to find similar listings.  Select customers receive an invitation via text to enable the service, while others can join a waitlist for future access.  Amazon’s expansion into text‑based AI shopping reflects the growing trend of consumer‑facing AI agents, a trend also being pursued by companies such as DoorDash.
key_points: Amazon introduces a text‑based Alexa shopping feature for select U.S. customers
Customers can search, add to cart, purchase, and manage lists via text messages

posts.title: Binance CFO is leaving to 'pursue a new venture' after $6.3 billion hack | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Binance’s chief financial officer Kaiser Ng is stepping down to pursue a new venture after more than five years at the exchange, following a $6.3 billion hack that saw users withdraw $3.6 billion after a temporary freeze. The company and the FBI have blamed a North Korean group called TraderTraitor for the breach, and Binance has pledged to cover all losses so users are not impacted. A transition plan has been in place for the last six months, and Ng will be succeeded by Justin Yek as CFO. The departure comes just a week after the high‑profile theft, underscoring the ongoing security challenges in the crypto industry.
key_points: Binance CFO Kaiser Ng departs after $6.3 billion hack
Binance will absorb stolen funds, protecting users
North Korean group TraderTraitor blamed for the breach
Justin Yek named as new CFO

posts.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: OpenAI has secured $11 billion in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion, according to Bloomberg. The round is still open and could ultimately raise about $20 billion, falling short of the earlier $30 billion target. OpenAI’s plans to go public have been delayed, with expectations now pointing to an IPO next year. The announcement comes amid a volatile AI market, heightened by political shifts and growing regulatory scrutiny of data centers.

The funding round could total $20 billion, below the earlier $30 billion target

posts.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: A Ramp report shows that AI spending has flatlined in August and September, with token spend rising only 1.5% while the previous month saw a 42% jump, even as token volumes continue to climb. The slowdown coincides with aggressive price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic, which have slashed API and model prices and offered enterprise discounts, turning the market into a buyer’s war. Investors are reacting to the data, with Anthropic’s valuation falling from an estimated $2 trillion to $1.2–$1.3 trillion and OpenAI’s valuation dropping to $1.25 trillion, raising doubts about the continued hyper‑growth narrative. The report suggests that while usage is up, companies are spending less per token and per employee, especially outside the top 1% of high‑growth firms, indicating a potential shift in revenue trajectories for leading AI providers.
key_points: AI spending grew only 1.5% in Aug‑Sep, a sharp drop from July’s 42% rise, despite higher token volumes.
Price wars and enterprise discounts from OpenAI and Anthropic have turned the market into a buyer’s war, stalling revenue growth.
Anthropic’s valuation fell to $1.2–$1.3 trillion and OpenAI’s to $1.25 trillion, reflecting investor concern over slowed spend.
Median firms spend $12‑$15 per employee per month, while the top 10% spend $600‑$1,000, showing a widening gap in AI spend intensity.

posts.title: Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Physicl, a new robotics‑AI startup founded by Alex de Vigan, has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to deliver high‑fidelity 3D simulations that help train robots more effectively. The company repurposes technology originally built for the e‑commerce rendering platform nfinite, turning real‑world data into physics‑accurate virtual environments. Its Studio product ships with 10,000 ready‑made scenes and 100,000 assets, enabling users to generate synthetic data for difficult edge cases such as identifying a cup on a cluttered counter. Early adopters like SpAItial are already using Physicl’s data to improve their Echo‑3 world‑model builder, underscoring the startup’s potential to bridge the gap between virtual training and real‑world performance.

posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Palo Alto Networks is reportedly negotiating to buy AI‑agent security startup Clutch Security for $500 million in cash plus milestone‑based payouts, a deal that would value the three‑year‑old company at roughly 50 times its $10 million annual recurring revenue. Clutch, which protects AI agents’ access to corporate systems, raised a $20 million Series A in January 2025 at an $85 million valuation. The acquisition would mark Palo Alto’s seventh purchase this year, underscoring the firm’s strategy of acquiring AI‑focused security innovations to counter rising AI‑driven cyberattacks. posts.title: Airbnb says it's launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Airbnb announced that its custom AI travel agent will launch in the first half of 2027, following a detailed explanation in its Q3 shareholder letter. The agent will use a generative‑UI approach, combining maps, photos, calendars and itineraries to create a personalized interface rather than a text‑heavy chatbot. CEO Brian Chesky emphasized that travel planning is aspirational and that the agent will support users throughout their trip, from booking to post‑stay assistance. The announcement coincided with strong Q3 earnings, a 19% revenue increase to $4.87 billion, and an upgraded 2026 growth forecast in the high teens.
key_points: Airbnb’s AI travel agent is slated for release in early 2027 and will feature a generative‑UI interface tailored to travel planning.
The agent will assist users beyond booking, handling changes, refunds, and 24‑hour safety support.

posts.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Security researchers uncovered more than 800 publicly exposed instances of the Chinese‑made AI hacking tool Artex, an open‑source autonomous penetration testing system that can launch attacks from reconnaissance to data exfiltration with minimal human input. The tool has been linked to several high‑profile cyberattacks, including a September assault on the Korean finance industry and an October breach of IT support giant ConnectWise that compromised Microsoft cloud customers. The findings highlight how misconfigured or unsecured deployments can expose both attackers and their targets, increasing the risk of widespread exploitation. Although Artex has announced a shift to closed‑source for paid customers, dozens of copies of its code remain available on code‑sharing sites and can still be used in active attacks.
key_points: Over 800 Artex instances were found publicly exposed on the internet without authentication
Artex has been used in major attacks against Korean finance firms and Microsoft cloud customers
Misconfigurations of the tool expose both attackers and victims, amplifying risk
The tool is moving to closed‑source, yet code copies remain freely available

posts.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Meta has unveiled Spaces, a new feature for its Muse agents that lets users create topic‑specific breakout conversations in the sidebar of the Muse interface. Spaces act as project tabs—such as vacation planners, recipe collections, or gift trackers—that Muse can build and maintain automatically, even integrating updates from third‑party apps. The launch follows the recent debut of Muse Voice, and Meta reports that Muse agents already have 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada. Zuckerberg highlighted the feature on X, demonstrating use cases like a BBQ game, event tracker, and home control dashboard.
key_points: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to create topic‑focused collaborative tabs for Muse agents

posts.title: After the midterms, is the AI industry in for a rough two years? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Theresa Loconsolo
posts.summary: The U.S. midterm elections, which saw Democrats win a majority of seats, are expected to bring tighter restrictions on data center development, as 41 ballot measures largely favored new limits. The outcome also signals increased scrutiny of Big Tech and AI firms, with lawmakers likely to push for more regulation across the industry. OpenAI is already rebranding its data center strategy in anticipation of these changes. The combined effect could create a challenging environment for AI companies over the next two years.
key_points: Democrats won a majority in the midterms, leading to stricter data center rules
Data center restrictions could hit AI firms like OpenAI
Increased government scrutiny may slow AI industry growth

posts.title: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build US factory | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: The Pentagon has granted a conditional $250 million loan to 6K, a 12‑year‑old battery startup, to build a Tennessee factory that will use a microwave‑powered process to produce cathode materials without relying on Chinese suppliers. 6K had previously received a $50 million Department of Energy grant that was rescinded by the Trump administration, forcing the company to reapply and delay its original 2024 opening. The new loan reflects growing U.S. defense interest in domestic battery production and the startup’s unique technology that can serve multiple battery chemistries, including lithium iron phosphate. The funding aims to bolster U.S. supply chain resilience amid shifting EV market dynamics.

posts.title: Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Fox has finalized its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, making the combined entity the third‑largest television business in the United States by viewership. The deal, announced in June and expected to close in the first half of 2027, wrapped up earlier than projected after a Justice Department antitrust review. Fox now gains access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households, which it plans to use to improve advertising targeting and strengthen its position in the fast‑growing connected‑TV market. Roku’s founder, Anthony Wood, said the company will continue to innovate with the support and resources of Fox.
key_points: Fox completes a $22 billion purchase of Roku, creating the third‑largest U.S. TV business by viewership.

posts.title: Serve Robotics launches new business to become the AWS for robots | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Serve Robotics, a maker of self‑driving sidewalk delivery robots that spun out of Uber’s 2021 acquisition of Postmates and went public in 2024, announced a new business line called Physical AI Services aimed at becoming the "AWS for robots." The company will offer connectivity and data tools—including Serve Link for high‑performance robot‑to‑AI system communication, a data curator for edge‑case identification, and a foundation‑model data catalog built from its own sidewalk fleet—to help other firms build robots for farms, warehouses, and other uncontrolled environments. Serve Robotics is also partnering with T‑Mobile to bring AI computing power closer to robots, while its delivery operations shift from Uber to partners such as DoorDash and Wonder. This expansion signals the company’s intent to monetize the technology it developed for its own robots while maintaining its core delivery businesses.

The new line includes Serve Link, a data curator, and a foundation‑model data catalog built from its sidewalk fleet

posts.title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: OpenAI has unveiled a new cybersecurity-focused model, ChatGPT Cyber, as part of its Daybreak Red program, offering advanced vulnerability hunting tools to top-tier users. Max Justicz, a security researcher, leveraged GPT‑5.6 Sol to uncover a severe Ubuntu server flaw that could let attackers seize control, prompting a patch from the Debian Project. OpenAI also reported finding 948 potential Linux kernel issues and 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities, underscoring the model’s scanning power. The launch has sparked debate over the balance between empowering defenders and the risk of enabling malicious actors, as well as concerns about resource allocation within the Daybreak initiative.

posts.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Underdog has released a 32‑megabyte text‑to‑speech model called Woof that can run entirely in a web browser without an internet connection, demonstrating that high‑quality voice generation is possible on consumer devices. The 31‑million‑parameter model is open‑source and downloadable, allowing users to keep their data private while still accessing advanced AI. A demo game featuring a retro‑tech room, a typewriter, and a music tuner showcases Woof’s capabilities and subtly criticizes cloud‑based models. Underdog also offers a 167‑MB speech‑to‑text model Bark and a 27‑billion‑parameter laptop‑ready model, positioning itself as a leader in edge‑AI solutions.

posts.title: Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Tesla announced that it will stop producing the Cybertruck in 2027 and will use the Texas factory to build Cybercab robotaxis, a move that signals a shift toward the company’s AI and robotics ambitions. The decision follows the Cybertruck’s disappointing sales—only tens of thousands sold in three years versus the 250,000‑per‑year forecast—along with higher-than‑expected price and reduced range. Tesla has already discontinued the Model S and Model X to free up production space for its Optimus humanoid robot, underscoring a broader strategy to prioritize robotics over traditional vehicle models. The move highlights Tesla’s willingness to pivot its product lineup in response to market performance and strategic priorities.
key_points: Tesla will cease Cybertruck production in 2027 and repurpose the factory for Cybercab robotaxis

posts.title: At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: At least ten local governments and police departments have dropped or are phasing out Flock Safety surveillance cameras since the summer, citing privacy, data‑sharing, and misuse concerns. The backlash reflects a broader pushback against rapid AI adoption, with cities like Monroe, Ohio, and League City, Texas, voting to terminate contracts and remove license‑plate readers. Flock, which offers license‑plate readers, drones, and gun‑shot‑detection devices, has more than 100,000 cameras nationwide, but the company has responded by shortening data retention to seven days and requiring case codes for database searches. While some municipalities, such as Cleveland, Ohio, are tightening restrictions rather than abandoning the technology, the trend underscores growing public skepticism about surveillance tools and the need for greater oversight.
key_points: Over ten U.S. cities have ended or are ending contracts with Flock Safety amid privacy and misuse concerns.

posts.title: The New York Times reportedly in talks to buy Letterboxd for $330 million | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: The New York Times Company is reportedly in exclusive negotiations to acquire the movie‑rating platform Letterboxd for $330 million. Letterboxd has surged from 3 million users in early 2021 to 28 million in April, with more than half of its audience under 35, and it projects earnings of about $15 million this year. The deal would value the company at roughly 22 times its annual earnings, a premium that reflects the Times’ interest in expanding its media footprint into film fandom. Film studios A24 and Sony had also shown interest, but A24 was priced out of the bidding.

The feature, introduced at Meta’s Connect conference, relies on new Muse Realtime Avatar and Voice models and presents an animated, customizable avatar nicknamed Jolly. It is available on mobile, web, and Mac, with plans to extend support to AI Glasses and a forthcoming Muse Charm wearable. Meta’s goal is to anthropomorphize the AI to deepen user connection and expand its ecosystem with a year‑end wearable device.

posts.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Meta president Dina Powell McCormick warned that the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections could make it harder for the company to build new data centers, citing a growing backlash against such facilities that is tied to broader concerns about AI. She explained that Meta’s strategy is to demonstrate tangible benefits to local communities—paying its own electricity, directing tax surpluses to teachers and first responders, keeping jobs local, and securing bipartisan support—to win approval. Meta has a 20‑year history of building data centers, currently operating in 23 states and planning several 1‑gigawatt or larger projects, and it hopes its AI investments, especially the consumer agent Muse, will drive future growth and monetization of its compute capacity. The company believes that by showing how AI can cure disease, expand education, and democratize technology, it can shift public sentiment and secure the infrastructure needed for its services.

posts.title: The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Stephen Ward, a former Secret Service agent who once turned a hacker into an informant, closed a $250 million first fund for Brightmind Partners in late 2023 and led a Series A that helped SGNL be sold to CrowdStrike for $740 million. He is now raising a second $250 million fund on his own after co‑founder Gur Talpaz departed, betting on a market where early‑stage cybersecurity startups are raising more capital than later‑stage ones for the first time in over a decade. Ward’s career path—from Coast Guard to Secret Service, to CISO roles at TIAA, Home Depot, and Insight Partners, and finally to venture capital—shapes his pragmatic, data‑driven exit strategy. The move positions Brightmind to capitalize on a surge in early‑stage cyber fundraising and the growing appetite for strategic exits in the sector.

posts.title: Aina's smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Hardware startup Aina has launched a $399 smart ring that combines a small screen, joystick, microphone, and speaker, allowing users to interact with AI agents and control both AI and non‑AI apps from their wrist. The ring, which goes on preorder on Thursday, adds gesture‑based controls and a speaker for calls, positioning it as a more feature‑rich alternative to existing smart rings like Pebble Index and Natura. Aina’s founder Apoorv Shankar said the device is designed for people surrounded by digital devices who need a better interface for proactive agents. posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Box announced a new feature called Box Content Retrieval that embeds Nvidia’s Nemotron model into its core product, enabling agents to answer queries faster and more accurately. The integration is expected to deliver four‑times faster responses, 20% fewer errors, and 90% fewer tokens used, according to Nvidia’s VP of generative AI software. posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Discovered Materials, a San Francisco startup in Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch, has announced a $1 million challenge to push AI models to solve five open problems in materials science, a field where physics is far more complex than mathematics. The company assembled an advisory panel of leading academics to define the problems and will award the prize pool to any team that provides a solution, while also using the effort to benchmark AI progress in this domain. The initiative reflects a shift toward AI‑driven scientific discovery, with Discovered Materials also aiming to develop industrially useful semiconductor materials within a year of its seed round.

posts.title: Sequoia hits rewind, undoing 20 years of expansion | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Sequoia Capital announced a sweeping restructuring in a memo titled "The Sequoia of Tomorrow," revealing that it has raised roughly $10 billion in new funds while simultaneously shutting its London office, ending its Arc accelerator and Scouts program, merging its early‑stage and growth teams, flattening its partnership structure, and canceling the Monday partner meeting. By concentrating on high‑conviction, highly selective investing, Sequoia aims to give more energy to fewer people and initiatives, hoping to better support founders as they move through stages. The memo acknowledges the cost of breaking successful programs and the potential pain of losing talent, but stresses the need to reinvent itself to keep pace with accelerating change.

posts.title: Claude can now analyze your spending with its new Personal Finance tool | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Anthropic has launched Claude’s new Personal Finance tool, allowing users to connect bank and credit‑card accounts through Plaid and ask the chatbot questions about their spending. The feature is read‑only, does not move or invest money, and keeps conversations out of the model’s training data. Claude can summarize monthly expenses, flag duplicate charges or unexpected fees, and explain financial concepts like APR. posts.title: India's EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country's rising microdrama market | TechCrunch

posts.title: Nothing CEO says company's mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek

While a firm release date has not been set, the announcement signals Nothing’s push into AI‑first consumer hardware.

posts.title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Uber reported that only four rides were booked through AI agents during its busiest week in October, and just 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by AI agents out of 320 million total trips and orders. The company’s CFO highlighted the limited traction, while CEO Dara Khosrowshahi expressed optimism that AI agents could boost demand across the platform. Despite the hype around personal AI assistants, the average booking time in Uber’s app is already short, so the time savings from agents are minimal. Uber remains bullish on the potential of AI agents, noting that the number of major assistants is growing and that many AI companies are engaging with the company.

posts.title: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Canva announced a 22% workforce reduction, cutting 1,271 employees, as it confronts a slowdown in growth after a decade of expansion. CEO Melanie Perkins explained that the company must reorganize, merge product, growth, and platform teams, and adopt a hybrid work model to streamline communication and broaden employee responsibilities. The layoffs also prompted Canva to revise its revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20% and saw its valuation drop to roughly $35 billion, reflecting rising AI costs and intensified competition from AI-driven design tools. Despite these challenges, Canva continues to develop its own AI models to lower dependence on third‑party services while navigating a market increasingly dominated by general‑purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini.

Canva lowered its revenue growth forecast to 20% and valuation to $35 billion due to rising AI costs.

posts.title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Ferrari’s first electric car, the Luce, designed by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, has sold out for its 2027 production run, with every planned vehicle already allocated to buyers and deliveries slated to begin in the fourth quarter. The 2027 model starts at about $615,000, and while Ferrari has not disclosed exact production numbers, it is expected to produce fewer than 500 units this year and aims for 2,500 units by 2030. Ferrari’s third‑quarter financials showed a 7% rise in revenue to €1.9 billion and a 13% increase in net income to €431 million, prompting the company to lift its full‑year adjusted earnings guidance to at least €3 billion. Customization sales, which account for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped drive the strong profitability and underscore the brand’s focus on personalized luxury.

posts.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Google announced that K‑12 schools using its education suite will lose access to Google Search unless they opt in to its AI tools such as Gemini, sparking immediate backlash from educators, politicians, and antitrust advocates. The company said the change is meant to give schools more control over AI use, but critics argue it coerces schools into adopting Google’s AI and threatens a monopoly over essential search services. Senators Bernie Sanders and Richard Blumenthal, former FTC chair Lina Khan, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the move as extortion and anticompetitive. Google has clarified that AI features are off by default and schools can enable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually while it develops a “Guided Learning” tool to help students learn rather than simply receive answers.

posts.title: Titan OS raises $46 million to expand its smart TV OS internationally | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Barcelona-based Titan OS raised $46 million in new equity and debt financing, bringing its total capital to $110 million. The funding, sourced from BlackRock‑managed debt facilities and existing investors Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners, will accelerate the company’s ambition to expand its TV OS into new markets and deepen partnerships with manufacturers and content providers. With 30 million users and a growing roster that now includes Philips, Sharp, AOC, Vestel, Skyworth, TiVo and Tubi, Titan OS positions itself as a monetization platform that offers advertisers access to a larger, AI‑enhanced audience. posts.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models' identity | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Anthropic has announced FlashProve, an open‑source system that uses cryptographic proofs to verify which AI model produced a given output. The system requires labs to publish a model fingerprint that can be matched to outputs without revealing internal weights, allowing users to confirm that responses come from the claimed model. FlashProve could prevent model swapping, protect commercial interests, and enable third parties to verify claims about model usage. The researchers released a technical spec and code on GitHub, but have no immediate plans to deploy the system.

posts.title: Ten years later, 'Pokémon Go to the polls' still haunts the internet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: During Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign, she referenced Pokémon GO in a rally, sparking the meme “Pokémon Go to the polls” that has resurfaced every U.S. election. The meme now serves as a reminder of how early‑internet culture—when Facebook, Twitter, and Tumblr dominated—has been replaced by AI‑generated content and a fragmented digital landscape. 2016 is nostalgically remembered as a “good year” for many, with Spotify playlists and Instagram posts spiking as people shared throwback content. The meme’s persistence across the political spectrum shows how humor and a call to vote can coexist in a cynical, algorithm‑driven era.

posts.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Some AI data centers are retrofitting retired jet engines to burn natural gas because grid connections and new turbines are taking years to come online. The converted units can be deployed in as little as 24 months, a stark contrast to the seven‑year timeline for a 100‑MW grid hookup in Northern Virginia. Companies such as xAI, OpenAI, and the Denver‑based Crusoe have already installed or ordered dozens of these engines, while others have abandoned larger turbine deals in favor of the quicker solution. Although the jet‑engine turbines are less efficient and more polluting than purpose‑built gas plants, they offer a short‑term fix that may become less attractive as efficiency and environmental concerns rise.

posts.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search | TechCrunch

posts.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz

posts.title: Apple Watch's AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple has begun beta testing its new Audio Intelligence suite on the Apple Watch, launching the features in the iOS 27.3 update for developers. The four opt‑in tools include sound and song recognition, Live Rewind—which lets users double‑press the crown to view a 15‑second text snippet of the last conversation—and Siri Recaps, which summarizes conversations into bullet points without recording raw audio. Apple emphasizes privacy by processing audio on the watch’s S11 chip, encrypting data in a secure enclave, and deleting summaries from its Private Cloud Compute immediately after use. The beta will later expand to a public test before the features become available to all users.
key_points: Live Rewind captures a 15‑second snippet of recent speech that can be saved or deleted after 30 seconds
Siri Recaps generates concise, speaker‑agnostic summaries that can be exported to Notes or Journal and are deleted after seven days if not saved
Audio is processed on the watch and iPhone in a secure enclave, with no raw audio stored or sent to Apple
The features are currently in developer beta via iOS 27.3 and will roll out to the public after broader testing

posts.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Trajectory, a Stanford‑born startup, has raised $45 million in a Series A led by Sequoia and backed by Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures, valuing the 18‑person company at $300 million. The firm offers a continual‑learning platform that lets businesses fine‑tune open‑source AI models with real‑world feedback, enabling lawyers, doctors, and other specialists to improve models without hiring costly research teams. By automating post‑training, Trajectory aims to make specialized AI deployment faster, cheaper, and accessible to nontechnical users. The platform is already used by companies such as Harvey, Rogo, Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia, and it competes with other post‑training startups like Thinking Machines Lab, Applied Compute, and Prime Intellect.
key_points: $45 million Series A at a $300 million valuation led by Sequoia with Nvidia, Bessemer, and Bain Capital Ventures
Trajectory automates continual learning so nontechnical experts can fine‑tune AI models with real‑world feedback
The platform is already adopted by firms in law, finance, and tech, speeding up specialized AI deployment

posts.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing...something with third-party AI apps | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Apple’s services division, already at record levels, is looking for new revenue streams amid regulatory pressure on the App Store and a slump in mobile gaming.  On its earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh hinted that AI could drive growth by encouraging customers to upgrade and by opening opportunities with third‑party apps and partnerships.  Investors are speculating that Apple could profit from distributing third‑party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.  Despite headwinds, Apple projects services growth of 8‑9% for the December quarter.
key_points: Apple may monetize third‑party AI agents via the App Store and take a revenue cut
Regulatory changes and legal challenges have reduced App Store commission revenue in key markets
Apple’s services business remains record‑level, with 8‑9% growth expected in the next quarter
AI is seen as a driver for customer upgrades and new partnership opportunities

posts.title: Germany says lawmakers' iPhones may have been hacked with spyware | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Germany’s federal cybersecurity office warned that members of parliament and other public figures may have been targeted by government‑backed spyware, following Apple’s threat notifications that iPhones could have been compromised. The BSI urged anyone who received a notification to assume their device might be infected, though it did not confirm which officials were affected or which state actors were involved. Apple’s alerts, which flag zero‑click exploits that can silently steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, have also reached users in 99 countries. The incident underscores the opaque supply chain of mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus from NSO Group, that governments often purchase to surveil political opponents.
key_points: German BSI warned parliament members could have been hit by government‑backed spyware after Apple’s threat alerts.
Apple’s notifications flag zero‑click exploits that can silently steal data, but do not confirm actual compromise or attribution.
The case highlights the use of private spyware vendors like NSO Group’s Pegasus, which many governments purchase.

posts.title: Snap settles lawsuit accusing platform of fueling teen depression and eating disorders | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Snap has settled a lawsuit filed by two teenagers who alleged the platform was designed to be addictive and contributed to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. The settlement is part of a broader wave of litigation targeting social media companies for their impact on young users, following similar cases against Meta, TikTok, and YouTube. Snap had already settled other cases scheduled for trial and had expected CEO Evan Spiegel to testify. The company says it has implemented safeguards, safety tutorials, and expert partnerships and remains committed to improving user safety and well‑being.
key_points: Snap reached a settlement with two teen plaintiffs over addiction and mental‑health claims.
The case follows similar lawsuits against Meta, TikTok, and YouTube.
Snap asserts it has introduced safety measures and will continue to strengthen them.
The lawsuit underscores growing legal scrutiny of social media’s influence on youth mental health.

posts.title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Ninja’s new Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer blends a 1,000‑W microwave with a 1,700‑W air‑fry system in a single unit, using FusionCrisp technology to heat food quickly while giving it a crispy finish. The appliance, priced at $449.99 (discounted to $349.99 on Amazon), features a 5.5‑quart glass dish, a non‑stick crisper plate, and no rotating plate, allowing larger dishes to be cooked at once. While it can replace separate microwave and air‑fryer units and free counter space for those who use both, its 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1‑inch footprint and high price make it less suitable for small kitchens or budget shoppers.
key_points: Ninja’s Crispi combines a 1,000‑W microwave and a 1,700‑W air fryer in one unit using FusionCrisp technology
The appliance costs $449.99 (Amazon $349.99) and measures 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, offering a large cooking area without a rotating plate
It can replace separate microwave and air‑fryer appliances, freeing counter space for users who regularly use both
Its high price and size make it less ideal for small kitchens or budget‑conscious buyers

posts.title: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: TechCrunch discusses how AI CEOs such as Marissa Mayer, Sam Altman, and Mark Zuckerberg have made out‑of‑touch remarks about AI’s role in everyday life, sparking criticism. The article questions whether the industry’s focus on optimizing basic human interactions—like dating, parenting, and social needs—really serves the average consumer. A podcast interview with Amanda Silberling explores whether the disconnect stems from marketing missteps, product design choices, or a mismatch between the CEOs’ target audience and the broader public. The discussion highlights growing skepticism about AI’s societal impact and the need for companies to balance innovation with genuine human connection.
key_points: AI CEOs have made remarks that many see as out‑of‑touch, prompting criticism.
The industry’s push to replace basic human interactions with AI may not align with everyday users’ needs.
Amanda Silberling argues the issue is partly marketing and partly product design.
There is increasing societal skepticism about AI’s role in personal and social life.

posts.title: Apple says it's 'hard to predict' when iPhone Duo constraints will improve | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple acknowledged that shipping delays for the iPhone Duo are still ongoing and it is difficult to predict when supply will meet demand, according to COO Sabih Khan on the company’s fiscal fourth‑quarter earnings call. The delays stem from extraordinary demand that caused the device to sell out within hours, coupled with rising memory‑chip costs driven by the AI industry. Apple has reluctantly raised prices on several products and is deepening its titanium partnership with Perryman to support the new foldable phone. Customers who missed pre‑orders are now facing delivery dates that extend into next year, prompting Verizon to offer gift cards as an apology.
key_points: iPhone Duo shipping delays push delivery into next year due to extraordinary demand and supply constraints
Apple has raised prices on several products amid soaring memory‑chip costs
Apple is strengthening its titanium supply partnership with Perryman for the foldable device
Verizon is compensating affected customers with gift cards

posts.title: Apple's inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple’s inventory rose sharply in fiscal Q4, jumping 31.1% from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion and growing 154.3% year‑over‑year. The surge is largely driven by higher memory chip costs, which the company expects to keep climbing and are a key factor behind its 45‑46% gross‑margin forecast for the December quarter. Apple is increasing memory purchases by $33 billion from June to September, while also raising device prices to offset the cost pressure. Weak iPad sales, down 10% YoY, were attributed to supply constraints amid the broader memory‑cost squeeze.
key_points: Inventory increased 31.1% in Q4 and 154.3% YoY, largely due to memory chip costs
Apple forecasts a 45‑46% gross margin for the December quarter, citing rising memory expenses
The company raised memory purchases by $33 billion from June to September and expects further cost rises
iPad revenue fell 10% YoY to $6.2 billion, reflecting supply constraints and weaker demand

posts.title: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Squarespace announced a 19% workforce reduction, cutting roughly 300 jobs, as part of a restructuring aimed at streamlining operations and positioning the company for future growth. The move comes amid a broader industry shift toward generative‑AI‑powered website builders, with rivals like Wix and Lovable raising significant capital for similar tools. Squarespace has been investing heavily in AI, launching Blueprint in 2024 and the upcoming Forma platform, and recently returned to private ownership after a $7 billion buyout. The layoffs signal the company’s effort to adapt to changing market dynamics while accelerating its AI strategy.
key_points: Squarespace is cutting about 19% of its workforce, roughly 300 employees, to simplify operations and accelerate growth
The company is investing in AI with products like Blueprint and the upcoming Forma platform
Industry competitors such as Wix and Lovable are raising large sums for AI‑driven website builders
The layoffs reflect a broader shift in web hosting toward generative‑AI tools and a need to stay competitive

posts.title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: The New York Times has filed a federal lawsuit against the privacy‑focused browser Brave, accusing it of scraping the Times’ copyrighted articles and distributing them to AI companies such as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. The suit, which also names the Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel, alleges that Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages with an unidentified crawler, bypassed paywalls, and blocked publishers’ ads while selling its own. The Times calls Brave a "supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content" and seeks an injunction and damages. Brave, founded in 2015 and having raised roughly $250 million, has not yet responded to the complaint.
key_points: The New York Times sued Brave for scraping and distributing its copyrighted content to AI firms.
Multiple other newspapers joined the lawsuit, all filed in Manhattan federal court.
The suit accuses Brave of building a massive web index, bypassing paywalls, and blocking ads.
Brave, founded in 2015 and raised about $250 million, has not yet commented.

posts.title: Y Combinator's Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan revealed that he spends between $100,000 and $200,000 a year on AI tokens to power a suite of agents that handle everything from coding to personal email and notes. He showcased 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub to demonstrate how agents can automate day‑to‑day tasks and even anticipate needs. Tan highlighted YC’s internal agent, Stray Light, which aggregates the entire founder database to streamline operations, and he warned that treating agents like static software limits their human‑like flexibility. He concluded that personal AI agents could become mainstream once costs drop, but cautioned against relying on free agents controlled by large tech firms that may impose algorithmic constraints.
key_points: Tan spends $100k–$200k annually on AI tokens to run a network of agents that manage both work and personal data.
He shares 23 Claude Code skills on GitHub to illustrate how agents can automate tasks and anticipate needs.
YC uses an internal agent, Stray Light, that compiles all founder data to improve operations.
He believes personal AI agents will become mainstream only if prices fall and users retain control over their own models.

posts.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Hinge is testing a lower‑priced subscription tier that adds extra filters and custom location boundaries, a move announced during Match Group’s Q3 2026 earnings call. The new plan is aimed at women and price‑sensitive users, as Match Group notes Hinge’s revenue per payer is nearly twice Tinder’s but its payer penetration is lower. Despite Hinge’s strong growth—12% YoY increase in global monthly active users, 19% rise in direct revenue, and 2.3 million paid subscribers—the company is shifting strategy to broaden its paying base amid widespread subscription fatigue. The initiative comes alongside Match Group’s broader efforts to diversify engagement with features like Group Hangouts, Events, and real‑time adaptive recommendations.
key_points: Hinge’s new tier adds filters and custom location boundaries to attract price‑sensitive users
Match Group highlights Hinge’s high revenue per payer but low payer penetration compared to Tinder
The shift follows a prior experiment with a higher‑priced tier and aims to convert more users into paying customers
Subscription fatigue remains a challenge, prompting additional engagement features such as Group Hangouts and real‑time recommendations

posts.title: A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe's supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: A second wave of cyberattacks targeted supermarket refrigerators across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden, raising temperatures and causing widespread food spoilage. Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks, which were carried out by changing defrost settings on Danfoss‑made units that no longer receive security updates. The incidents follow a similar French attack last month and highlight how weak IoT security can disrupt the food supply chain. The attacks underscore the real‑world impact of cyber threats on everyday infrastructure and consumer goods.
key_points: Hackers raised temperatures on Danfoss refrigerators, causing food spoilage in multiple European countries
Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed heavy losses and the manipulation of defrost settings
Earlier France and US UNFI attacks show a growing trend of IoT‑based supply‑chain disruptions
Weak cybersecurity practices in IoT devices enable real‑world damage to food and logistics

posts.title: 2 days till Founder Summit in Boston | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch’s Founder Summit will kick off on November 4 at 9:00 a.m. ET in Boston’s SoWa Power Station, bringing founders, investors, and operators together to discuss scaling and growth. The event, presented by Fidelity Private Shares, features breakout and roundtable sessions, with keynote speakers Steve Fredette of Toast and Chase Garbarino of HqO sharing Boston‑based success stories. Attendees can network through Braindate, roundtables, and side events that deepen connections across the local startup ecosystem. It’s the final day to secure tickets before prices rise, with a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free pass and other group discounts expiring soon.
key_points: Founder Summit starts Nov. 4 at SoWa Power Station and is the last chance to buy tickets before price hikes
Key speakers Steve Fredette (Toast) and Chase Garbarino (HqO) will share Boston‑centric scaling insights
The agenda includes breakout sessions, roundtables, Braindate networking, and side events to connect founders, investors, and operators
Buy‑one‑get‑one‑free ticket deal and group discounts expire on the event day
